hook_text: Thirty torn triangles. Thirty straight edges. Not one gap.
clip_script:
A teacher hands every learner a sheet of coloured paper and a ruler and says: draw any triangle you like, as big as the page allows, and cut it out. Thirty triangles appear — long thin ones, fat ones, one almost a right angle, one with an obtuse corner so wide it looks like a slice of pie.

Then: tear off the three corners. Not cut — tear, so the pieces are ragged and nobody can say they were measured. Now put the three corners together on your desk with their points touching at one spot and their edges meeting.

Thirty desks, thirty results, and on every one the three torn corners fit together to make a straight edge. A half-turn. The three interior angles of any triangle add to 180 degrees, and the parallel line through the apex explains why they always must.
visual_style: Ragged paper corners sliding together at a point into a perfect straight edge, then a triangle with a parallel line through its apex and two alternate-angle arcs swinging up
call_to_action: Open the full session to investigate the triangle angle facts and use them with reasons.
